Persuasion, Deception, and the Same Scatter Plot

DSC 106 Project 2 · Spring 2026 · Maxime Chung, Sana Gupta, Rose Park
Dataset: World Bank Human Development Indicators, 1960–2020

Proposition

“Wealth does not buy health: getting richer has not made countries healthier.”

Two visualizations argue each side of the proposition (four total). Every chart on this page draws from the same World Bank dataset; the headline cross-section (179 countries, 2019) is reused across both pro and con first charts so no country is added or dropped between sides. The persuasion lives in design choices: axis scaling, fitted curves, residual framing, time-series slicing, annotations, and titles. The pro side's second chart even uses the con side's own regression line as its starting point, to argue that 30% unexplained variance is a 20-year gap, not a rounding error.

Scoring scale: each design decision is rated −2 (fully deceptive) to +2 (fully earnest), in 0.5 steps.

Pro side: two visualizations arguing wealth does not buy health

Pro 1 Wealth is no cure

All 179 countries plotted on a linear GDP-per-capita axis. No fit line. Outlier countries that contradict the wealth-equals-health intuition are highlighted to draw the eye away from the broader trend.

Design decisions

  1. −1.5
    Linear x-axis on GDP per capita. GDP across countries spans almost three orders of magnitude, so on a linear axis ~90% of countries collapse into a vertical wall on the left. The Preston curve becomes invisible. We considered a square-root scale and rejected it as too obvious a deceptive move.
  2. −1.5
    Cherry-picked outlier highlights. Four "rich-but-sick" countries (Equatorial Guinea, Nigeria, Lesotho, Eswatini) and four "poor-but-healthy" countries (Vietnam, Nicaragua, Honduras, Bangladesh) are colored red and green. These eight points are the largest residuals against the trend; highlighting only outliers pushes the reader to read "no relationship" rather than "strong relationship with notable exceptions."
  3. −1
    No fit line, no R². A regression line would reveal R² = 0.70 and undercut the argument. Omitting the fit forces the reader to read the cloud by eye, where the linear axis already obscures the relationship.
  4. −1.5
    Slanted title and inset callout. "Wealth Is No Cure: At Every Income Level, Health Outcomes Are All Over the Map" and the Equatorial-Guinea-vs-Argentina inset prime the reader to look for variation rather than trend before they engage with the data.
  5. −0.5
    Y-axis truncation at 50 years. The full range is roughly 53 to 85. Starting at 50 (rather than 0 or 60) compresses the visible vertical spread slightly and makes the cloud look more disorderly. Mild but it is the same family of choice the assignment prompt flags as a typical deceptive move.

Pro 2 The 20-year gap that wealth does not explain

The pro side accepts the con side's regression line on its own terms, then plots the residuals — how far each country's actual life expectancy lands from what its GDP predicts. Even granting R² = 0.70, the unexplained 30% spans nearly twenty years of life. Equatorial Guinea is sixteen years below its predicted life expectancy; Vietnam is seven above. Wealth alone clearly does not buy health.

Design decisions

  1. +2
    Use the opposing side's own regression line to compute residuals. We did not invent a new model. We took the con side's published log-GDP fit and plotted what it leaves out. Steel-manning, not strawmanning, and the most earnest move in the project. A reader cannot dismiss the chart by saying "your model is wrong" because the model is the opponent's.
  2. −1
    Show only top and bottom 12 residuals; collapse the middle 155. The middle band of countries the model fits well gets compressed into a single gray annotation. This suppresses the visual presence of the 87% the model predicts well and elevates the 13% it misses. Showing all 179 lollipops became unreadable and self-defeating for the argument.
  3. −0.5
    Diverging red/green palette. Red and green carry pre-cognitive "bad/good" associations that load the chart emotionally before the reader processes magnitudes. Mild deception because the encoding also does genuine work (negative vs. positive residual).
  4. −1.5
    Title frames the unexplained variance as a "20-year gap." The 20-year figure is the actual range from worst to best residual, but the framing converts a statistical residual into a humanitarian indictment. We chose this because residuals alone are emotionally inert.
  5. +1
    Disclose R² = 0.70 in the subtitle. The chart explicitly tells the reader that the model explains 70% of variance. A more deceptive version would have buried this number. Disclosing it makes the chart fall or stand on the interpretation of the unexplained 30%.

Con side: two visualizations arguing wealth does buy health

Con 1 The strongest pattern in development

The same 179 countries, the same year, the same variables. The only changes from pro chart 1 are: a logarithmic x-axis, a fitted regression line with R² disclosed, a 95% confidence band, five reference countries marked along the curve, and a title that takes the opposite stance.

Design decisions

  1. +1.5
    Logarithmic x-axis on GDP per capita. GDP per capita is exponential across countries; log is the conventional and expressive encoding. It distributes the points evenly and reveals the Preston curve. Earnest in itself, even though the contrast with the pro side's linear axis exposes how much weight the axis choice carries.
  2. +1
    Fitted regression line with R² disclosed. The fit (life expectancy = 9.9 × log10(GDP) + intercept, R² = 0.70) is shown explicitly in the legend. Plotting the fit and disclosing R² lets the reader judge how strong the relationship is.
  3. +0.5
    95% confidence band around the fit. The shaded band gives an honest sense of the residual spread. Mildly deceptive because a casual reader may not notice that several countries fall outside the band entirely; pro chart 2 makes those countries the whole story.
  4. −1.5
    Slanted title and inset callout. "The Strongest Pattern in Development: Richer Nations, Longer Lives" frames a correlation as a near-deterministic rule. The relationship is real and strong, but the language pushes past what a single-year cross-section can prove.
  5. −0.5
    Annotated only countries that anchor the trend. Five countries (Ethiopia, India, China, US, Japan) are marked along the curve. They span the full income range and sit close to the fit, which trains the eye to see the chart as a curve rather than a cloud. Asymmetric attention rather than asymmetric data.

Con 2 Six decades, every country bends the same way

A 2019 cross-section is vulnerable to the critique that maybe rich countries just happen to be old. The con side answers with a longitudinal panel: take six anchor countries spanning the full GDP range (Ethiopia, India, China, South Korea, US, Japan) and trace life expectancy and GDP per capita from 1960 to 2019. As GDP climbs, life expectancy climbs alongside in every panel for sixty years. Gains range from +9 years (US) to +33 years (China).

Design decisions

  1. +1
    Same y-axis range across all six panels. Identical 28 to 88 year limits make magnitudes comparable across countries. Ethiopia's gain reads as visually as dramatic as China's. We considered per-panel auto-scaling and rejected it because it would have flattened Ethiopia and inflated the US in a way that distorts the actual story.
  2. +1
    Logarithmic GDP on the secondary axis. GDP per capita rose by orders of magnitude in some panels (China $200 to $8,000). Linear GDP would crush most trajectories into an early flat line. Log is the appropriate encoding for a multiplicative variable.
  3. −2
    Hand-picked six countries with strong upward arcs. The most deceptive move on the con side. Russia in the 1990s, Zimbabwe in the 2000s, Venezuela in the 2010s, and the entire Soviet collapse would each show life expectancy falling as GDP fell or stagnated. Choosing six poster children turns a real but messy correlation into a triumphal narrative. The title compounds this with "every path."
  4. −1
    Title overclaim: "every path bends toward longer life." The chart shows six paths; the title implies all paths. Most readers will not audit the sample. We considered "Six countries" as the title and rejected it as insufficiently emphatic — exactly the kind of choice that pro chart 1 critiques.
  5. +0.5
    Annotation showing total life-expectancy gain per country. Each panel carries an explicit "+9 yrs life", "+33 yrs life" badge. The numbers are real and correctly computed. The only slant is that the comparison is across countries that all gained, not against countries that lost.

Final reflection

The hardest part of this project was committing to plot the same data on both sides of the cross-section. Once we did, the rhetorical machinery became visible. The pro and con first charts share every single data point. The proposition flips because of the x-axis scale, a fitted curve we drew or did not draw, and a title we wrote. Working in this constraint clarified what counts as a deceptive technique versus a fair editorial choice: a log axis is not deceptive, a linear axis is not deceptive, but choosing one of them while writing a title that depends on the reader not noticing the choice is. Pro chart 2, which uses the con side's own regression line to surface the residuals, was the most satisfying chart to build because it argued from inside the opponent's premises rather than swapping them out.

What surprised us was how much of the persuasion lived in things we did not draw. Pro chart 1 is persuasive partly because there is no regression line on it. Adding the same R² = 0.70 line that appears on con chart 1 would single-handedly undo pro chart 1's argument. That asymmetric omission is, in some ways, more dishonest than any positively misleading element of either chart, because nothing on the page would obviously flag it. Con chart 2 was the inverse temptation: hand-picking six countries whose trajectories all bent the right way produced a gorgeous, monotonic story that is also the project's biggest lie of omission. Russia in the 1990s and the post-Soviet life-expectancy collapse would have made our title false, and we never showed those countries.

Our working definition of ethical visualization is this: a chart is ethical when the reader, given enough time, would still accept the framing — the axes, the fits, the annotations, the country selection, and the title — as a defensible reading of the data. A chart is misleading when its persuasive force depends on the reader not having that time. The line we draw between persuasion and deception is exactly the line between framing choices we would defend in public to a critical reader and framing choices that need the reader's inattention to survive. By that test, pro chart 2 is the most ethical visualization in this project (it uses the opponent's own model and discloses R²), and con chart 2 is the least (it claims "every path" while showing six handpicked ones). All four are persuasive, but they are not equally honest about it.

Methodology & data validation

  • Source files: World Bank Human Development Indicators, specifically economy-and-growth.csv and social-development.csv.
  • Indicators: GDP per capita (constant 2010 US$); life expectancy at birth, computed as the unweighted mean of the male and female series. The World Bank's population-weighted total LE differs by ~0.1 years and does not change any conclusion drawn here.
  • Time slice: charts 1 on each side and pro chart 2 use the 2019 cross-section. Con chart 2 extends to a 1960–2019 panel for six countries.
  • Country universe: 179 entities for which both GDP per capita and life expectancy are non-null in 2019. Aggregate rows ("World", "OECD members", regional groupings) excluded.
  • Joins and nulls: source files contain zero duplicate (Country Name, Year) rows. Inner-join then drop nulls on both indicators. Identical filter applied to all four charts.
  • Fit: OLS of life expectancy on log10(GDP). Slope = +9.9 years per 10× increase in GDP, R² = 0.70. Reused across con chart 1 (visualized) and pro chart 2 (residuals).
  • No jitter applied to any scatter point. Every dot on Pro 1 and Con 1 sits at its true 2019 GDP and life expectancy. We considered jittering low-GDP countries to declutter the left wall on Pro 1 and rejected it as undisclosed deception. The crammed left side is the chart's argument; relocating points would have falsified the claim.
  • Subagent-assisted design: the second visualization on each side was specced by a "data-scientist" subagent persona (definition sourced from awesome-claude-code-subagents-main/categories/05-data-ai/data-scientist.md), spawned via the Agent tool. The analysis pass used the data:validate-data skill (zero duplicate keys, 12 country values spot-checked, R² confirmed at 0.70).
  • SWD chart helpers applied to every render: all four final charts use swd_style(), action_title(), and the check_label_collisions(fix=True) auto-fix pass from helpers/chart_helpers.py. This produced consistent typography, a single accent palette, and algorithmic resolution of every detected label overlap. The detector resolved 4 collisions on Pro 1, 1 on Con 1, and 0–1 on the others; the script prints the counts on each run.
  • Reproducibility: generate_charts.py at the repo root, with helpers under helpers/, regenerates every chart on this page from the source CSVs.
